data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: The National Bank moved to inflation targeting in 2015 alongside a free float of the tenge, after years of a managed peg. Inflation was 17.2% in 2008, moderated to 5-8% in the early 2010s, then spiked to 14.6% in 2016 after the tenge's 2015 devaluation, easing to 5.3% by 2019. The 2022 shock drove it to 15.0% (14.5% in 2023), and the IMF projects 11.4% for 2025, still well above the 5% target. Dollarization and administered prices complicate transmission, and the central bank has kept policy tight to rebuild credibility.
debt_management: Public debt is low and has stayed so: 6.7% of GDP in 2006, rising only to 26.4% in 2020 on COVID and to a projected 24.6% in 2025. The sovereign wealth fund (Samruk-Kazyna/National Fund) is the real fiscal buffer, absorbing oil windfalls; the 2022 surge took GDP to $225.5bn and a projected $302.8bn by 2025. Banking-sector cleanups (notably after the 2009 BTA default) were handled off the sovereign balance sheet. Debt sustainability is comfortable; the issue is the non-oil deficit and fund drawdowns.

key_events.event: Banking crisis; BTA Bank's 2009 default was one of the largest emerging-market restructurings.
Commodity boom took GDP to $133.4bn before the crisis hit.
Oil collapse and Russian ruble crisis forced the tenge float in August 2015; inflation hit 14.6% in 2016.
Nazarbayev resigned after three decades; Tokayev succeeded him.
January unrest ('Bloody January') shook the regime; oil windfall then repaired finances.
Diversification and Middle Corridor trade pushed GDP toward a projected $302.8bn.

outlook_next_decade: Kazakhstan's base case is solid: moderate debt, large buffers, and growth from oil, uranium, and transit trade, with inflation hopefully converging to target. Risks are oil-price dependence, the political transition's durability after 2022's unrest, and exposure to Russia (trade, the Caspian pipeline, secondary sanctions). If diversification and governance reforms advance, upside is real; if oil falls and buffers are drawn down, the old vulnerabilities return. Debt is not a constraint.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
